pages.description: Anchored by the historic city of George Town, the Malaysian state is a melting pot of influences in one of the most picturesque places on the planet.
pages.text: How to Eat Your Way Through Penang, Malaysia's Island of Hawker Stalls and Street Art | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD Find Out Why Penang Is Asia’s Most Exciting Emerging Region Anchored by the historic city of George Town, the Malaysian state is a melting pot of influences in one of the most picturesque places on the planet. Traditional Chinese lanterns hang in front of the Acheen Street Mosque in George Town, the capital city of Penang. Chris Schalkx, Kintzing By Kristin Braswell Published October 20, 2026 Separated by a narrow strip of sea, the Malaysian state of Penang has dual personalities: On Penang Island, travelers can explore the historic streets of George Town, the capital city, before heading to rainforest-fringed beaches. On the mainland Seberang Perai, across the Penang Strait, traditional villages and winding mangrove rivers sit alongside industrial hubs. Chinese, Indian, Burmese, Arab, and European immigrants have shaped the cuisine, architecture, and religious identity of Penang, which was once a key trading post linking the Pacific and Indian Oceans. In George Town today, luxury hotels are housed in former Chinese merchant family estates, well-preserved colonial buildings, and narrow alleyways lined with murals and street food hawkers, giving the city a metropolitan pulse. In 2027, George Town's Penang Hill Cable Car will begin gliding from the Penang Botanic Gardens to the top of Penang Hill in less than 10 minutes, revealing panoramic vistas of rainforest canopies. pages.description: Iceland’s capital lives up to the country’s nickname — the Land of Fire and Ice — with geologically rooted cultural curiosities, bathing pools, bars and restaurants
pages.text: How to Experience Iceland's Fire and Ice in Reykjavík | National Geographic TRAVEL How to Experience Iceland's Fire and Ice in Reykjavík Iceland’s capital lives up to the country’s nickname — the Land of Fire and Ice — with geologically rooted cultural curiosities, bathing pools, bars and restaurants The design of Hallgrímskirkja, Reykjavík’s main church, is said to have been inspired by the country’s mountains. Getty By Daniel Stables Published October 22, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The world’s northernmost capital, Reykjavík is a culturally vibrant city, home to around one third of Iceland’s population. Yet, it still feels close to the duelling forces of nature that define the country’s life and landscape: glaciers and snow-capped mountains above ground; and an infernal volcanism seething below the surface, heating geothermal pools and hot springs. Clues to this unique dynamic are everywhere in Reykjavík. It runs almost exclusively on geothermal power — the only capital city in the world to do so. The tap water, naturally filtered through mazes of volcanic rock, is preternaturally pure and good for the skin (you’ll soon get used to the slightly eggy, sulphurous smell). Galleries host displays of artwork hewn from glacier ice, while immersive exhibits take you deep into the belly of the Earth. Some of the country’s most spectacular bathing pools are found right here, too, ensuring your time in Reykjavík will be, quite literally, immersive. pages.description: Polo ponies, palace hotels and oysters on ice: the Snow Polo World Cup St Moritz returns every January for two days of high-altitude glamour. Here’s how to make the most of it.
pages.text: How to Experience St Moritz’s Snow Polo World Cup Weekend | National Geographic By Emma Al-Mousawi Published November 14, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). For one weekend in late January, frozen Lake St Moritz, encircled by Switzerland’s snow-heaped Engadin Alps, becomes the glittering stage for one of polo’s most prestigious events: the Snow Polo World Cup St Moritz. Sunglass-clad spectators in cashmere, elegant coats and designer puffer jackets gather as champagne flutes clink and oysters are shucked. On the ice, six teams of white-slacked players thunder across the 200-metre pitch, competing for the coveted trophy against the dazzling backdrop of one of Europe’s oldest and most exclusive ski resorts. Polo traces its origins back more than two millennia to the grasslands of Persia, but its snowy incarnation is decidedly younger. It was conceived here just over 40 years ago by Reto Gaudenzi, a local player and founder of Switzerland’s first polo team. Undeterred by the fact that polo had never been played on snow, he experimented with hoof grips and a larger, slower orange ball. A successful trial followed in 1984; a year later, the world’s first snow polo tournament was staged on the lake before more than 1,000 spectators. Today, the three-day event draws crowds of 26,000 — and dozens of private jets. Forty grooms tend 120 ponies in heated stables, while three daily matches unfold on snow-covered ice at least 50cm thick. pages.description: Passengers aboard the Ultramarine can feel the Arctic wind on their faces as they get up close with Greenland’s biggest glaciers — and even take a plunge into the Atlantic’s icy waters.
pages.text: How to Explore Greenland by Luxury Expedition Ship | National Geographic TRAVEL How to Explore Greenland by Luxury Expedition Ship Passengers aboard the Ultramarine can feel the Arctic wind on their faces as they get up close with Greenland’s biggest glaciers — and even take a plunge into the Atlantic’s icy waters. Quark Expeditions’ heli-hiking trips use helicopters to reach remote hiking routes in southern Greenland. Michelle Sole, Quark Expeditions By Adrian Phillips Published November 6, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). “If you fall in, you’ll be there for thousands of years,” says a watchful guide as I crawl to the edge and stare into oblivion. The hole, drilled through the glacier by its own meltwater, is hundreds of metres deep. It’s part of an ice sheet two miles thick that covers 700,000sq miles of Greenland. Few come to this wilderness of sudden storms and treacherous crevasses. It’s mainly tough-skinned adventurers, seasoned Inuit hunters — plus a handful of tourists like me. Such an otherworldly spot is, for the first time, within reach of tough-skinned and soft-skinned alike. Our ship — the Ultramarine — has a pair of twin-engined helicopters that extend its reach far beyond the fjords of southern Greenland. “I like to pretend you’re holding gin and tonics,” says our smooth-talking helicopter pilot, after flying seven miles north from the ship and landing on the glacier with the gentlest of thuds. “There now. pages.title: How to Explore the Indian Ocean Through Its Spices | National Geographic
pages.description: Once among the world’s most valuable commodities, spices transformed the Indian Ocean, enriching empires while weaving together the cultures, cuisines and communities of distant shores. Today, travellers can still follow those ancient routes through fragrant plantation visits, cooking classes and market tours.
pages.text: How to Explore the Indian Ocean Through Its Spices | National Geographic By Daniel Stables Published September 19, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Nowadays, most of us take spices for granted — a pinch of cinnamon in porridge, black pepper over pasta or cumin stirred into a curry. Yet for centuries these everyday ingredients shaped the course of history. The trade in black pepper facilitated cultural and economic intermixing between ancient Rome and India, while camels pulled frankincense caravans across the deserts that separated Africa and Asia, taking with them ideas, recipes, music and language. Today, these influences can still be felt in many countries, offering a fascinating, and often delicious, theme through which to explore a place. Browse the Spice Souks of Muscat, Oman Located on the Arabian Sea between Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the UAE, the seafaring nation of Oman has long been a link between East Africa, India and Southeast Asia. That story is told in the spice section of Muttrah Souk, the Omani capital’s historic covered market, where technicolour cones of powdered ginger, turmeric and cumin sit alongside piles of frankincense rocks, bundled strands of saffron, and less familiar items like loomi — black, sun-dried limes. The air hangs particularly heavy with the scent of frankincense, which Omanis use to perfume their homes, cars and traditional robes. pages.text: How to Explore the Pantanal | National Geographic A school of fish and a hungry caiman in the waters of the Pantanal region Photograph by Luciano Candisani, National Geographic TRAVEL How to Explore the Pantanal Explore the Pantanal from all corners with this guide to the beauty of this national park and UNESCO World Heritage site. By Avery Stonich Published August 4, 2016 • 4 min read The Pantanal is the world’s largest wetland , pooling over 81,000 square miles (210,000 square kilometers)—an area nearly the size of Kansas—in the center of South America, mostly in central-western Brazil and straddling the borders of Paraguay and Bolivia. Often overshadowed by the Amazon to the north, the Pantanal quietly harbors the highest concentration of wildlife in South America . It’s part national park and part UNESCO World Heritage site , and it’s considered a critical region of the world by the World Wildlife Fund, which estimates that 325 species of fish, 159 species of mammals, 656 species of birds, 53 species of amphibians, and 98 species of reptiles live in this hotbed of biodiversity. Cattle in the marshlands of the Nhecolandia region, Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil Photograph by Yann Arthus-Bertrand, Getty Images If You Go The Pantanal teems with life in every season. The dry season, July to October, is the best time to see mind-boggling concentrations of wildlife clustered around water holes. pages.text: How to explore the tropical side of Japan in Okinawa | National Geographic TRAVEL How to explore the tropical side of Japan in Okinawa With its laid-back seafaring culture and unique wildlife, the Yaeyama archipelago in Japan’s far southern Okinawa prefecture reveals a different side to Japan. The traditional Okinawan sabani boats were historically used for fishing and travelling between islands. Photograph by James Whitlow Delano By Georgia Stephens Published January 7, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). It’s show time. Up heaves the sail, a concertina of heavy canvas pulled taut against the creaking wooden mast. It gulps the breeze that’s whisking cotton puffs of cloud out to sea. Black butterflies, big as sparrows, rise from the steep jungle at our backs as the droning of cicadas meets the surf raking the beach. The air is flower-scented, hot and heavy as water. Up comes the anchor, out come the paddles; the nose of the traditional sabani boat plunges into the waves. Any sailor leaving Ishigaki island needs to be absolutely certain of their course. Head north west, and the next landfall lies hundreds of miles away in China; east, and it’ll be the considerably farther-flung shores of Mexico. Here, in southern Okinawa Prefecture, Japan fizzles out in a spray of its remotest isles. Closer to Taiwan and the Philippines than the mainland and fed by warmer currents, the subtropical Yaeyama Islands, of which Ishigaki is a part, are unique within Japan. pages.text: How to Explore the U.K.’s Most Haunted Destinations | National Geographic TRAVEL Explore the U.K.’s Most Haunted Destinations With a long history of hauntings, mystery and witchcraft, the UK is bedevilled with wicked destinations. Photograph by Alamy By Connor McGovern Last updated October 30, 2026 • 8 min read This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The UK is riddled with stories of the macabre, morbid and mysterious. How many of them are true is another matter, but there's no denying the strange pull of the chilling spots where many of them took place. More than just stages for ghostly goings-on, many of these historic locations — castles, churches, pubs and even the landscape itself — have played host to significant historical events and witnessed tragic human tales unfold, all giving rise to intriguing stories that still captivate us today. Garreth Gibbs By Sarah Barrell Published April 20, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Scattered as if on a pirate’s map off England’s southwesterly tip, the Isles of Scilly aren’t a place you stumble over. Travellers need to have booked well ahead for the short, spectacularly scenic transfer by twin-prop plane or helicopter from Penzance to the 140-strong archipelago. Or embark on a three-hour, dolphin-flanked ferry, which plies azure waters towards show-off shelves of pristine white sand. It’s a pilgrimage richly rewarded by a landscape of palms, lipstick-pink sea thrift and sky-blue agapanthus flowers, framing sand-blown, barely-there roads. Beyond St Mary’s, the largest and most populous isle, there are few cars on the four other inhabited outposts of Tresco, Bryher, St Martin’s and St Agnes. They offer a daily invitation to hike and island-hop, with dockings dictated by the tides, and crossings taking mere minutes on jetboat ferries with names like Firethorn and Thunder. Vesterålen Kysthotell sits right on the water in Stokmarknes. Justin Foulkes, Getty By Daniel Stables Published April 19, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). From its mountainous national parks to its scenic rail journeys, Norway has so many highlights, it’s hard to know how to begin planning an itinerary. Thankfully, though, this is a country where simple pleasures are available wherever you end up and whatever your budget, from bracing dips in the crystal-clear waters of a coastal fjord to overnight stays in a remote forest hut. Knowing how to get around and how best to make the most of your money are two essentials for unlocking all the country has to offer — read on to discover these and more tips for creating your perfect trip. How do I get there? Norway’s main international airport, Oslo Gardermoen, has direct flights from London, Manchester and Edinburgh on carriers including Norwegian , British Airways and SAS . You can also fly direct to Bergen and Stavanger from the UK. Norway is connected to the rest of Europe by train, with overnight services between Oslo and Copenhagen, Stockholm and Gothenburg. pages.description: A five-day drive from sandy bays to lake-rimmed mountains is ample time to get the measure of Australia’s smallest state — a land of bounty, both on the plate and in the wilderness.
pages.text: How to plan the ultimate road trip through Tasmania | National Geographic By Justin Meneguzzi Published June 19, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Home to the Aboriginal Palawa people for 40,000 years, Tasmania was settled by Europeans from 1803. They found a maritime climate, volcanic soils and some of the cleanest air in the world. These bountiful conditions have since helped the apple-shaped island build its reputation for producing superlative wine, whisky and cheese. On a road trip across Australia’s smallest state, preserved colonial-era towns and farms seem to appear around every corner, while mountains and valleys knitted together by walking trails provide chances to stretch your legs. Meanwhile, after centuries of oppression, the Palawa people invite visitors to connect with their ancestral homelands through the sights, sounds and flavours of the bush. You could easily drive coast to coast in six hours, but why rush? Tasmanians know that having patience and adopting a slower pace are key to enjoying the finer things in life. Plan up to a week for a road trip from the coast to the high country, starting in the historic southeastern port city of Hobart, Tasmania’s state capital, and finishing in the northerly hub of Launceston. Along the way, make time to savour a drop of local whisky, perhaps sample oysters from a coastal farm fringed by white sand, head into the backcountry for a day’s wilderness walk, or spend time foraging with Aboriginal guides. pages.text: How to Plan the Ultimate Sri Lankan Adventure | National Geographic By Berkok Yüksel and Lorna Parkes Published November 4, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Palm-fringed surf bays, tea plantation hikes, ancient ruins and incense-filled temples — few islands can match the diversity of Sri Lanka. First-timers tend to head south for beach-hopping and safaris, but the developing north offers an equally rich experience, along with an insight into the island’s Tamil culture. Here are two handpicked itineraries that show off the best of both sides of the island. Highlights of the South A classic circuit of the country’s southern half takes in highland tea plantations, Buddhist pilgrimage sites and heritage towns — as well as some of its finest surf hubs. 1. Kandy Best For: Temple Pilgrimages The last stronghold in Sri Lanka to fall to the British in 1818, Kandy was once a royal seat and remains an important cultural and religious centre. Enthroned in the lush highlands, the city has a large lake at its heart, with royal bathhouse ruins, tiny bee-eaters in the trees and vendors selling chilli-mango at its edges. Pilgrims come from all over the Buddhist world to attend the thrice-daily puja (worship) ceremony at the Temple of the Tooth, a bone-white complex that holds a relic of Buddha himself, protected by bristling walls of elephant tusks. pages.text: How to Save the World’s Largest Lemurs? Listen to Their Songs. | National Geographic ANIMALS How to Save the World’s Largest Lemurs? Listen to Their Songs. Scientists are employing AI-guided bioacoustics monitoring to discover how many critically endangered indri still exist in Madagascar's forests. A male indri sings in Madagascar. These endangered lemurs have complex vocals that help them claim territory in the forest. Photographs by Filippo Carugati By Sruthi Gurudev Published October 22, 2026 The tropical rainforests of Madagascar are a raucous wash of sound, pierced by astonishingly loud, musical singing. These are the vocalizations of the indri , the largest species of lemur in the world. Emanating from up in the green-black canopy, the indri songs are notably mournful and resonant—partly whale song and partly wolf howl. They rise to a crescendo and then fall away into silence. For roughly 88 million years, Madagascar has been geographically isolated from Africa and Asia. Considered something of an “ evolutionary sandbox ,” the ancestors of many of its terrestrial mammals are thought to have reached the island from continental Africa, some floating on mats of vegetation carried by ancient ocean currents. Once there, isolated populations proliferated and diversified, producing unique wildlife found nowhere else on Earth. The indri is one such animal. Endemic to the island, the species is critically endangered ; they’re threatened by habitat loss caused in part by tavy , the slash-and-burn agriculture that destroys their arboreal habitat. Thanks to its northern latitude and clear night skies, Edmonton is a prime spot to view the auroras. Explore Edmonton By Brendan Sainsbury Published May 12, 2026 Nature’s most spectacular light show, the Aurora Borealis, will be even more dazzling this year. This is thanks to a phenomenon called the ‘solar maximum’, defined as the ‘peak’ of the sun’s activity over its 11-year cycle. One of the best places to take advantage of this astronomical event is in Edmonton — North America’s most northerly city, set at latitude of 53.5ºN. With a landscape of wide-open plains, Edmonton and the surrounding region offers a front-row seat to the wonders of the galaxy. Here’s how to spot the auroras using Alberta’s capital as your base. When should I go? Though the solar maximum technically occurred in 2024, this high period of solar activity is expected to continue well into 2026. Put simply, this means that the sun will be sending more electrically charged particles to Earth than usual. These then convert to green, red, purple and blue light when they collide with our atmosphere, which we see as the auroras. Drawing visitors since the 1700s, North Norfolk has long been a place of escapism. You arrive ready to fill your lungs with sea air and let your gaze drift to the horizon. The natural beauty here is not the kind that smacks you in the face and overwhelms with superlatives. The expansive beaches, endless skies, fenland and watery network of the Broads are a more subtle tonic for the soul — you don’t have to work too hard to forget life beyond this somewhat overlooked patch of East Anglia. It’s also a place to get closer to wildlife. Many of the salt marshes in Norfolk offer some of Britain’s best birdwatching, while seals love to sunbathe on the shingle spits at Blakeney Point. Plus, there’s bluebell and snowbell carpets in spring, dragonflies buzzing over lavender fields in summer and woodland ablaze in ochre, yellow and red in autumn. Beyond the pull of its natural attractions, North Norfolk is dotted with stately homes, sliced through by heritage railways and framed by historic towns. Add it all together and you have a region that promises the kind of serenity many search far and wide for, yet few expect to find so close to home. It’s notoriously difficult to cultivate and painstaking to pick, so why are the world’s top chefs so hooked? Angelita Eriksen is the CEO and co-founder of Lofoten Seaweed. Max Emanuelson By Ally Wybrew Published November 17, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). “We call that the smell of money,” grins Tamara Singer, in response to my scrunched-up nostrils. To me, the aroma wafting my way smells less like endorphin-inducing ‘dosh’ and more like what it is: dehydrating fish corpses. ‘Pungent’ doesn’t quite cut it. I’m picking my way down the rocky shores of the remote Lofoten archipelago in Norway’s Arctic Circle, trusting my footing to the woolly-hat-wearing, wetsuit-clad co-founders of Lofoten Seaweed, Tamara and Angelita Eriksen. As we walk, I can’t take my eyes off the macabre scene: hundreds of stockfish hang from the hjells (wooden trellises) lining the road while row upon row of empty racks stand between them. I ask how many fish are hanging here. “There used to be a lot more,” Tamara says, her response subdued. The large gaps in the racks speak volumes about the state of an industry that was once the economic backbone of the country. On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models. South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market. But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China. This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. Stepping out, National Geographic Explorer Gina Moseley breathed deeply and took in the commanding view of Greenland ’s barren landscape. To the south, a frozen lake stretched out for miles, eventually giving way to brown and gray plateaus, interrupted by the white flash of glaciers in the distance. In the other direction, some 560 miles beyond the horizon, was the North Pole. The only other human presence was the helicopter pilot and the other passengers: Moseley’s life partner and this story’s photographer and fellow National Geographic Explorer, Robbie Shone, and technical climbing specialist Chris Blakeley. The weather was mild, just above freezing—perfect, actually—but Moseley knew that storms could blow up at a moment’s notice, bringing dangerous winds and dense fog. In such a case, they’d have to leave immediately or risk being stranded in one of the world’s most remote and forbidding environments. They were poised on the edge separating potential disaster and sublime discovery. Paul Bauer, Wien Tourismus By Ellen Himelfarb Published October 12, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). On 11 November, Vienna’s palaces and music halls kick into high gear. Dance floors swarm with couples waltzing in choreographed swirls — and freestyling to live electropop. The two scenes are complementary halves of the Austrian capital’s modern ball scene: an old custom attracting new attention, buoyed by social media and miles of bias-cut silk. The festivities trace their roots to the 1700s, when Emperor Joseph II opened the Hofburg Palace dances — until then, reserved for nobility — to ordinary citizens. The decision paved the way for a wider ball culture to develop in the following centuries. Public dancing venues expanded, professional groups began holding their own balls and the dances became key fixtures in the city’s social calendar — a tradition that continues to this day. When Gen Z came of age, they box-stepped into Ballsaison (ball season) fuelled by a penchant for retro style and, crucially, posting the pageantry online. But captain Dewi Lake summoned the words that inspired a first win over New Zealand in 73 years. With a rousing speech, the captain reminded his players of the feeling in the same changing room 12 months earlier, when they trailed by just three points at the break only to eventually lose 52-26. "Dewi made a very good point, the last time that we played them we had been in the contest, but let the dam break," Leicester and Wales wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb told the Rugby Union Weekly podcast. The Census Bureau will notify you in advance if you are in a survey, provide different ways to respond, and may follow up with you. We notify you if you are in a survey. The U.S. Census Bureau typically sends an official letter describing the survey for which your household or business has been selected and why your participation is important. This letter describes what the survey is, what type of questions will be asked, and what you can expect as a survey participant. For household surveys, most mailings from the Census Bureau are addressed to “the resident of.” Household surveys from the Census Bureau are only mailed to residential addresses, not to P.O. Boxes. P.O. Boxes are not associated with specific addresses, so the Census Bureau cannot use them as a mailing destination. If you are visited by a field representative working on a survey and have not yet received a survey letter or notice from the Census Bureau, you can request one from the representative at your door. You may also contact the Census Bureau Regional Office for your state for more information. Some surveys send invitations via text message or email. pages.text: How you can still explore the ancient city of Troy | National Geographic TRAVEL How you can still explore the ancient city of Troy Travel back in time to Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey through an ongoing excavation of the site believed to be the legendary city. A facsimile of the Trojan Horse in the port city of Çanakkale, Türkiye, draws travelers and fans of the epic Greek poems. dinosmichail, Alamy By Nick Hilden Published July 17, 2026 Driving south out of the petite port town of Çanakkale, on the northwestern tip of Türkiye, signs for “Truva” and “Troya” begin to appear with growing frequency. The bustle of modern life gives way to the pastoral, and half an hour later, you’re in the ancient city of Troy, some 3,000 years in the past. A towering wooden horse greets you at the gate and all around are scattered ruins, the Aegean Sea in the distance, and the plains upon which the legendary Trojan War was fought in between. “The aura is so strong, [that] when Caesar visited Troy he said, ‘Every stone has a name,’” says Rüstem Aslan , a professor at Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University , who has spent 40 years excavating the UNESCO World Heritage site believed to be the legendary city. Today, Hisarlik—Turkish for “ place of fortresses ,” the name for the hill where the ruins lie—recounts its history through the Troy Museum and the remains of architectural structures containing the echoes of Homer ’s great epic, The Odyssey .
